content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors present a meta-meta-learning system to model the within-lifetime acquisition of novel cognitive tasks. The outermost level functionally mimics evolution using basically ES-MAML (evolution strategies for gradient-based meta-learning, (Song et al., 2019)). content.title: Reply to reviewer
content.comment:
> The authors present a meta-meta-learning system to model the within-lifetime acquisition of novel cognitive tasks. The outermost level functionally mimics evolution using basically ES-MAML (evolution strategies for gradient-based meta-learning, (Song et al., 2019)). 

As pointed out in Appendix F3, ES-MAML could indeed be used in the two "top" loops. Here we use evolution with differentiable plasticity, because it allows more flexibility for evolution to fashion the meta-learning algorithm itself (as opposed to simply finding an initialization for backprop). In the revised Discussion we explain that this choice is motivated in part by Sutton's "bitter lesson" conjecture: putting as much as possible under control of optimization and learning tends to beat hand-design in the long run.

> The main ideas behind the model are not novel, although the combination of all components in a meta-meta-learning setting may be.
Evaluation is too limited, as the model is tested on a single overly simplified setup (e.g., stimuli and responses are always binary), and no baseline is provided.

As explained in the common reply and in the revised submission, the simplification of stimuli is precisely the crucial element which allows the system to work. It abstracts away perceptual processing, but preserves the requirement for working memory and cognitive  manipulation (which must be learned in the outer/middle loop), allowing the system to run for many generations in acceptable time. 

As discussed in the paper (Appendix A), the reviewer is correct that most of the underlying methods have indeed been used for standard meta-learning before, some of them by ourselves. What is new is their combination into a common mechanism, to not just meta-learn this or that specific cognitive task, but actually produce a self-contained agent capable of automatically acquiring novel cognitive tasks (i.e. meta-tasks). To our knowledge, while several authors have postulated the possibility and interest of such a meta-meta-learning process, no such method has been demonstrated before.

Our results show not just that such a multi-level optimization is possible, but also that it has practical importance (compare Figures 2 and A2, and see Section 3.3, Discussion, and Appendix B).

Given the lack of comparable results in the literature, we suggest the "baseline" here would be what happens without the meta-meta-learning framework. This is shown in Figure A2 (using a standard two-loop meta-learning), which shows a failure to acquire the tasks. To our knowledge there is currently no example of optimizing a self-contained meta-learner in the literature. We have updated Section 3.3 and the Discussion and added an Appendix C to clarify this point.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a biologically-motivated learning system capable of learning at three timescales: the network initialization and plasticity parameters (slowest scale), the plastic weights (middle scale) and the activations of the recurrent network (fastest scale). The authors demonstrate the capability of the system on the set of neuroscience tasks proposed by Yang et al (2019).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
The paper proposes the interesting idea of meta-meta-learning: learning a learning algorithm that itself learns a learning algorithm. The proposed method is well-motivated and could potentially be made biologically-plausible. Moreover, the discussion and experimental analysis are quite strong. The authors extensively demonstrate the properties of their method on the Yang 2019 tasks, particularly with the cross-temporal decoding.

**Weaknesses**
It is unfortunately unclear to me whether the setup really constitutes meta-meta-learning. As I understand it, the authors argue that each episode itself requires learning as opposed to simple stimulus response. They compare each trial of a Yang 2019 task to Omniglot. Indeed, I agree that Omniglot could be implemented in the setup of a Yang 2019 task (by, for example, within each episode sequentially displaying several Omniglot letters from an alphabet and then asking the network to classify unseen letters). However, the simple binary stimuli used by the authors make the resulting task appear more similar to a simple stimulus-response scenario (akin to MNIST) rather than requiring learning within each episode (like Omniglot). Can the authors concretely separate learning from merely applying a rule, and if so, can they demonstrate that there is learning within the recurrent activations of each episode vs. simply carrying out a rule? If not, I would suggest experimenting on a task that does really require learning within each episode.

Moreover, it is unclear to me if there is significant novelty in the learning system proposed by the authors given that many prior works have proposed meta-learning the parameters of a plasticity rule or a network initialization. Conceptually, what is the difference between the proposed work and applying MAML (Finn et al.) for example to a recurrent neural network (both would be capable of learning over 3 different timescales)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Quality**
The quality of the technical and empirical results is high. The technical decisions made by the authors are well justified, and sufficient details are provided regarding quantitative experiments.

**Clarity**
The work is quite clear. The figures are well illustrated and the discussion is comprehensive.

**Originality**
The work is unfortunately only marginally original in my opinion. The authors aim to demonstrate learning over three timescales, but unfortunately it does not appear that the Yang 2019 tasks are good candidates to demonstrate learning over these scales due to the simple rule-like nature of each episode. Moreover, the proposed learning system does not have significant novelty since previous meta-learning systems have proposed meta-learning parameters of a plasticity rule or a network initialization. See the weaknesses section above for more details.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is well-written and and the theory and experiments are solid. However, the main weakness of the paper is its unfortunately marginal significance: it is unclear whether the work really proposes a new type of task compared to prior meta-learning literature, and moreover the proposed method appears similar to prior work.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Reply to reviewer
content.comment:
> It is unfortunately unclear to me whether the setup really constitutes meta-meta-learning. As I understand it, the authors argue that each episode itself requires learning as opposed to simple stimulus response. They compare each trial of a Yang 2019 task to Omniglot. Indeed, I agree that Omniglot could be implemented in the setup of a Yang 2019 task (by, for example, within each episode sequentially displaying several Omniglot letters from an alphabet and then asking the network to classify unseen letters). However, the simple binary stimuli used by the authors make the resulting task appear more similar to a simple stimulus-response scenario (akin to MNIST) rather than requiring learning within each episode (like Omniglot).

We refer the reviewer to our common reply above: the tasks are not just analogous to Omniglot, one of the tasks is actually exactly identical to a Harlow task with 2 trials per episode. This should confirm the meta-learning nature of the tasks used here, despite the extreme simplicity of the stimuli.

The MNIST task is a good example of  a purely reflexive, stimulus-response task. To solve MNIST, the agent  must learn to produce one fixed response for any given stimulus. By contrast, in each episode of the tasks used here, the agent must memorize successive stimuli, manipulate them in some way, and produce a response. 

In addition, the precise "manipulation"  to be applied depends on the actual task, and must be learned by trial and error in an outer loop of successive episodes (in our case, the "middle" loop of 400 episodes per lifetime) - as in standard meta-learning.

As  the  reviewer points out, our model makes use of maximally simplified stimuli, abstracting away all perceptual processing. This choice maximizes computational efficiency, allowing us to run many generations in reasonable time with ordinary resources. This abstraction of perceptual processing allows us to concentrate on the actual process of "learning to cogitate" itself, that is, learning a mental manipulation  to be applied to information stored in memory, rather than a reflexive response to a perceived stimulus. 

The success of our model in endowing an agent with this ability is demonstrated in Figure 2, which shows that after evolution, the agent automatically learns a simple, but not trivial mental manipulation task ("same or different") that it has never  encountered during its  evolution. We note that  this particular withheld task is exactly the one that we show is identical to the 2-trial Harlow task in the common reply.

(Note that some tasks in Yang's original framework are *not* cognitive / meta-tasks -  e.g. the "reaction time" tasks that require no memory. In our adaptation, we have taken care to only use tasks that do require some amount of working memory and  processing)

> Moreover, it is unclear to me if there is significant novelty in the learning system proposed by the authors given that many prior works have proposed meta-learning the parameters of a plasticity rule or a network initialization. Conceptually, what is the difference between the proposed work and applying MAML (Finn et al.) for example to a recurrent neural network (both would be capable of learning over 3 different timescales)?

As discussed in Appendix A, most of the underlying methods have indeed been used for standard meta-learning before, some of them by ourselves. What is new is their combination into a common mechanism, to not just meta-learn this or that specific cognitive task, but actually produce a self-contained agent capable of automatically acquiring novel cognitive tasks (i.e. meta-tasks). Since we operationally define "cognitive" tasks as a type of meta-learning task, this immediately implies the existence of three levels of learning. Trying to shoehorn this process into a standard two-loop meta-learning process fails (section 3.3, Figure A2). We have tried to make this point clearer in the introduction.

Our results show not just that such a multi-level optimization is possible, but also that is has practical importance (compare Figures 2 and A2, and see Section 3.3, Discussion, and Appendix C).

Regarding MAML: as mentioned in Appendix F3, Evolutionary-MAML or some first-order MAML algorithm might indeed be used in the top two levels, with the bottom two levels then implementing meta-learning by backprop training of a recurrent network, as in RL^2/Learning to Reinforcement Learn (original MAML would be unworkable as it would require backproping over the whole 400 episodes). We chose instead to use differentiable plasticity with evolution in the outermost loop, in part to preserve as much biological plausibility as possible, but also because this choice allows maximal flexibility to the optimization process: evolution has much more control over the design of the meta-learning algorithm, as opposed to merely choosing an initialization for backprop.

content.summary_of_the_paper: By combining current methods of continual learning, namely (activity+plasticity) and (plasticity+evolution), the authors proposed a framework in which a self-sustained network can learn a novel, unseen task by being trained on other cognitive tasks throughout evolution. Specifically, learning happens through synaptic plasticity across trials within a generation, and through changing innate weights and plasticity coefficients across generations.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:s
- Learning rules and objectives are clearly defined and well explained
- Clear writing and communication

Major weaknesses:
- Figure 2: Even after 1000 generations, it still takes ~150 trials for the model to learn the withheld task, which is much less efficient than current one-shot or few-shot learning paradigms in transfer learning. Does it ever get to a point where the model can learn the withheld task in just a few trials?
- Related to previous comment: In section 2.4 you described the “the mean error over the last 100 trials of both lifetime blocks is used as the loss $L_i$ for each individual for generation”. What would happen if you change the number of trials counted towards the loss, eg. 200 trials instead of 100? What about all 400 trials? Would that help the model learn in a few-shot manner?
- In section 3.2, the results communicated verbally in the first two paragraphs (i.e. increase in performance is not simply due to a mere indiscriminate increase in overall plasticity; did not detect obvious structure in the evolved weights or plasticity parameters) would be better communicated with figures
- In section 3.2 the last sentence “this confirms that all three learning systems are necessary for this model to succeed”. This statement can only be supported with separate ablation studies for each of the three components; however, the only ablation experiment was removing the $\Pi \odot \textbf{P}$ term, which includes both evolution and plasticity.
- Due to the model setup (i.e. no “lifetime loop” described in appendix section D.4), the paper could not address catastrophic forgetting since in each generation the task is randomly drawn. It would make the paper much stronger if this issue was addressed. In addition, it would also be interesting to explore how tasks related to one another (eg. some tasks are more “similar” to one another) and how this affects learning.
- In general, to me it seems the only novelty this paper provides was the “evolution loop”, where a set of “meta” parameters, PI and W, are trained with evolutionary strategy. But you can always create a more meta training loop with another set of meta-meta-parameters and perhaps another objective function. Will using another method in the outermost loop other than evolutionary strategy change the results? If it doesn’t, then the evolution metaphor would seem a little far fetched.

Minor weaknesses:
- The vocabulary is a little confusing at times, because in this paper words such as individual/generation/population/lifetime and block/task/episode/trial/batch are used interchangeably. I do appreciate the evolution metaphor, but I think a direct table of translation or comparison with machine learning terminology would be helpful for readers.
- Section 3.3 t1 and t2 the numbers should be subscripts
- Typo in Figure A3 legend: “from (not fro) neural activities”
- Page 8 section 3.3 in the main text “we perform this analysis both for at generation 0 and generation 1600” do you mean generation 1000? This error repeated a few lines below too.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The work is clearly communicated with high quality writing. The idea of evolution in meta-learning is relatively novel. Code would be needed to ensure reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: I'd lean slightly towards rejection: indeed paper provides much potential for an evolution-inspired learning framework, but simply adding loops seems not very innovative; and the results shown in the paper are quite sparse.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.title: Reply to reviewer - part 1
content.comment:
> Figure 2: Even after 1000 generations, it still takes ~150 trials for the model to learn the withheld task, which is much less efficient than current one-shot or few-shot learning paradigms in transfer learning. Does it ever get to a point where the model can learn the withheld task in just a few trials?

As pointed out in our general reply, the individual tasks are meta-learning tasks (e.g. withheld DMS task is exactly equivalent to a simplified Harlow task with 2  objects and 2 trials per episode). 

Therefore, the 400 trials are not equivalent to the few-shots or one-shot of a single episode: they constitute the whole outer loop of a meta-learning algorithm! They should be compared with the many thousands of episodes that are typically used for the outer loop of typical meta-learning experiments.

The reason why the meta-learning after evolution is relatively fast is, first, the strong simplification of the stimuli,  which abstracts away the need for perceptual processing; but also the fact that the evolutionary process has a endowed the agent with meta-learning abilities that are specifically tailored to this particular universe, and exploit its regularities to allow for fast acquisition of meta-learning tasks. This is analogous to how meta-learning itself allows for fast learning in each new episode of the task.


> Related to previous comment: In section 2.4 you described the “the mean error over the last 100 trials of both lifetime blocks is used as the loss  for each individual for generation”. What would happen if you change the number of trials counted towards the loss, eg. 200 trials instead of 100? What about all 400 trials? Would that help the model learn in a few-shot manner?

This  would be the equivalent of measuring the performance of a meta-learning algorithm by integrating episodic performance over the entire meta-learning process. This might have some drawbacks, e.g. discouraging (meta-)exploration. Empirically, in early pilot experiments we found that using performance over the last 100 trials to guide evolution worked well. 


> In section 3.2, the results communicated verbally in the first two paragraphs (i.e. increase in performance is not simply due to a mere indiscriminate increase in overall plasticity; did not detect obvious structure in the evolved weights or plasticity parameters) would be better communicated with figures

We agree with the reviewer. We have added a figure showing the final evolved innate weights and plasticity coefficients, for the same run used for the decoding experiments (Figure A4). 


> In section 3.2 the last sentence “this confirms that all three learning systems are necessary for this model to succeed”. This statement can only be supported with separate ablation studies for each of the three components; however, the only ablation experiment was removing the  term, which includes both evolution and plasticity.

We point out that Figure 2 shows what happens at generation 0 -  i.e. if we do not use any evolution (no learning occurs). As for the third system, because the tasks require working memory, it follows that they could not be performed by a memoryless system.

> Due to the model setup (i.e. no “lifetime loop” described in appendix section D.4), the paper could not address catastrophic forgetting since in each generation the task is randomly drawn. It would make the paper much stronger if this issue was addressed. In addition, it would also be interesting to explore how tasks related to one another (eg. some tasks are more “similar” to one another) and how this affects learning.

While the current set of tasks is sufficient for successful evolution, including multiple tasks per lifetime would require a larger set of tasks. We are currently working to implement more tasks from the Yang framework. With a larger set of tasks, we agree that studying multi-task lifetimes (and the possible emergence of continual learning systems) is of great interest.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The submission aims to simulate meta-learning or learning to learn at multiple scales of abstraction within a biologically plausible framework. To do so, the work couples an evolutionary optimization algorithm with a neural plasticity rule, producing a population of learners that is able to acquire held-out tasks from the neuroscience-inspired task set of Yang et al. (2018).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#### Strengths: 

1. **Intriguing motivation.** The submission aims to simulate meta-learning or learning to learn at multiple scales: (1) An evolutionary time scale, implemented as the modification via an evolutionary optimization algorithm of some initial connectivity parameters in a continuous-time recurrent neural network; (2) a timescale of learning across episodes, implemented as the modification of synaptic connections via a specific plasticity rule; and (3) a timescale of learning within an episode.

2. **Clarity**. The manuscript is very clear, and I had no trouble understanding all details of the setup.
Drawbacks of the experimental setup (with respect to the larger ambitions in the introduction) are straightforwardly discussed, though only in the latter half of the manuscript.

#### Weaknesses:

1. **The framework does not address _meta_-meta-learning**. The submission claims to address multiple scales of learning-to-learn, in contrast to prior work that addresses only "meta-learning" (e.g., learning within a task at the same time as learning across tasks). However, the framework depicted in Figure 1 and described in the text itself addresses only two scales of learning: an outer loop (evolutionary optimization of initial connectivity) and an inner loop (plasticity rule). Within an episode ("the episode loop"), no overt learning occurs (though the model is stateful as a recurrent network). As such, the framework is analogous to standard meta-learning.

2. **The contribution of the work needs to be clarified.** It is not clear exactly what to take from the paper. We see a setup motivated by biologically plausible learning rules applied to a task set that is simplified from an already simplified, low-dimensional neuroscience task set. Many models could likely solve this modified task set, though the paper does not provide any evidence to this effect or the contrary—no baselines are reported. The paper does not provide more specific insights that could be taken from the work to inform understanding, e.g., of the computational principles of learning to learn at multiple timescales. The submission deflects this by claiming that "Exploring the structure of evolved representation is an important objective for future work," but such an exploration could add something beyond a demonstration that "this works."

3. **Framing of "cognitive tasks" does not appear necessary.**
The submission claims that "cognitive tasks" are those that "...require acquiring, storing and exploiting a certain unpredictable piece of information from the environment for each new instance of the task." The word "cognitive" does not seem appropriate here, as it suggests anything relating to cognition and not this narrow definition of what seems to describe a task of "learning to learn ." I do not understand why this new terminology needs to be introduced except to make the problem setting appear distinct from the standard meta-learning problem setting.

4. **Important prior works are not discussed.**
Similar framings of multiple scales of learning have already been discussed in:

    [Wang JX. (2021) Meta-learning in natural and artificial intelligence. Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences. 38, 90-95.](https://authors.elsevier.com/a/1cTXd8MqMif3bO)

    The submission does not discuss much existing work in computational simulations of the interaction of learning and evolution; for example:
     
    [Hinton, Geoffrey E.; Nowlan, Steven J. (1987). "How learning can guide evolution". Complex Systems. 1: 495–502.](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/absps/evolution.htm)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The manuscript is very clear and I had no trouble understanding all details of the setup.
Drawbacks of the experimental setup (with respect to the larger ambitions in the introduction) are straightforwardly discussed, though only in the latter half of the manuscript.
content.summary_of_the_review: The dual motivations of studying learning to learn at multiple levels, beyond the standard meta-learning setup, and placing learning to learn within a biologically plausible framework, are of interest to the community. However, the framework presented is analogous to standard meta-learning, and the paper does not appear to provide insights about computational principles of learning to learn at multiple timescales, beyond that a particular meta-learning algorithm can solve this relatively simple task set.

content.title: Reply to reviewer - part 1
content.comment:
> The framework does not address meta-meta-learning. The submission claims to address multiple scales of learning-to-learn, in contrast to prior work that addresses only "meta-learning" (e.g., learning within a task at the same time as learning across tasks). However, the framework depicted in Figure 1 and described in the text itself addresses only two scales of learning: an outer loop (evolutionary optimization of initial connectivity) and an inner loop (plasticity rule). Within an episode ("the episode loop"), no overt learning occurs (though the model is stateful as a recurrent network). As such, the framework is analogous to standard meta-learning.

As stated in the common reply, we believe this is not correct. The innermost (trial/episode) loop involves the same type of learning as the Omniglot and Harlow meta-tasks, but with maximally simplified stimuli, allowing for fast computation and a sizeable variety of possible meta-tasks. We show this by pointing out that one of the tasks is exactly identical to a Harlow task with 2 trials per episode (see also Appendix E).

To our knowledge, the automated design of an agent capable of acquiring any such tasks through its own learned (evolved) machinery has not been demonstrated before.

 
> The contribution of the work needs to be clarified. It is not clear exactly what to take from the paper. We see a setup motivated by biologically plausible learning rules applied to a task set that is simplified from an already simplified, low-dimensional neuroscience task set. Many models could likely solve this modified task set, though the paper does not provide any evidence to this effect or the contrary—no baselines are reported. 

If we understand the reviewer correctly, they suggest that a standard meta-learning model, meta trained on these tasks, could produce an agent capable of acquiring such tasks, making our model redundant. 

If that is what the reviewer means, then we *do* offer some evidence - namely Figure A2, which shows the same experiment but with plasticity disabled. 

This control is exactly equivalent to a typical, two-loop meta-learning experiment, with RNN evolution in the "inner loop" (combining our inner  trial/episode loop and our middle lifetime loop over trials/episodes), and evolution in the outer loop (gradient descent cannot be used in the outer loop here due to the length of the "inner loop").

It doesn't work (Figure A2). The agent cannot even learn the evolution tasks, much less acquire the withheld test task.

We believe this negative result is evidence for the practical importance of the concept of multiple loops. As we point out in the Introduction, the Discussion, and Figure A6, there really are three levels of learning in this experiment (episodic, task, and evolutionary). When we try to shoehorn this on a standard two-loop meta-learning system, one loop (the RNN) is forced to perform two levels  at the same time (within episode learning of  episodic task-relevant information, and learning the structure of the task between episodes), which is evidently beyond its capacities. By contrast, by acknowledging the three learning loops and introducing an evolvable plasticity system (optimized by evolution between lifetimes, and optimizing the RNN between episodes),  the exact same model now produces an agent capable of acquiring these tasks.

We have rewritten the relevant sections to make this point clearer (Section 3.3 and 4.1, Appendix C).




> The paper does not provide more specific insights that could be taken from the work to inform understanding, e.g., of the computational principles of learning to learn at multiple timescales. The submission deflects this by claiming that "Exploring the structure of evolved representation is an important objective for future work," but such an exploration could add something beyond a demonstration that "this works."


Regarding understanding computational principles: the decoding experiments in Figures 3 and A3 represent precisely an attempt to understand the representations, how they change through an episode, and how they are modified separately by both evolutionary and within-lifetime learning. We welcome further suggestions about experiments to better  understand the dynamics of learning at multiple levels  in the system.

I do not understand why this new terminology needs to be introduced except to make the problem setting appear distinct from the standard meta-learning problem setting.

The ability to automatically acquire novel *cognitive* behaviors, as opposed to mere reflexive (stimulus-response) behaviors, is the actual point of the paper!  This is the ability we want our evolved agents to have. Meta-meta-learning and learning loops are a convenient framework to investigate this problem, rather than the goal per se. We have tried to rewrite much of the paper, especially the Introduction and the Discussion, to make this point clearer.

We agree that the definition of "cognitive" we use here (tasks that require storing and manipulating information, i.e. working memory) represents only one type of cognition. This definition has the advantage of being easily to operationalize: whether or not a task requires memory and manipulation of past stimuli is in general reasonably objective  and unambiguous. Another advantage is that they are by definition meta-learning, learning-to-learn tasks, allowing us to use  the framework of meta-learning to describe them. 




>  Important prior works are not discussed. Similar framings of multiple scales of learning have already been discussed in: Wang JX. (2021) Meta-learning in natural and artificial intelligence. Current Opinion in Behavioral Sciences. 38, 90-95. The submission does not discuss much existing work in computational simulations of the interaction of learning and evolution; for example:  Hinton, Geoffrey E.; Nowlan, Steven J. (1987). "How learning can guide evolution". Complex Systems. 1: 495–502.

We agree with the reviewer that this work is highly relevant. We have included citations of Wang 2021, as well as other authors who have proposed multiple nested loops of learning, each designing or optimizing the other (Introduction, Discussion, and Extended Related Work in Appendix A). Indeed, our overall framework here is very similar to Figure 2 in Wang 2021, where each loop would not just inscribe priors or constraints upon the lower one, but actually design the learning process itself. 

We believe our results strongly validate this (and similar) works, by proving that these processes are 1) feasible and 2) can have very tangible practical importance: As seen from the difference between Figure 2 and A2, considering the multiple learning loops in a learning experiment may produce a very large difference in performance (see Section 3.3, Appendix C).

replying_to: Replying to Learning to acquire novel cognitive tasks with evolution, plasticity and meta-meta-learning

content.title: General reply to reviewers
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments. We have tried to address their concerns in a revised version of the paper. We have thoroughly rewritten the paper (especially the Introduction and Discussion) to clarify our objective and contributions, added Figures (A4) to document the result of the process, and Appendices (A, C and E) to better explain our results and situate them in the context of the existing literature, in addition  to various smaller corrections. We believe the new version has been considerably improved by the reviewer's observations.

We have replied to each reviewer in detail below. Here we would like to make two comments that seem relevant to all of the reviewers' responses.

* First, we would like to clarify our overall objective. We are trying to design a self-contained agent capable of automatically acquiring novel "cognitive" tasks. Here we operationally define "cognitive" tasks as  those that require acquiring, storing and manipulating some unpredictable piece of information for each new instance of the task. We note that such tasks are, by definition, meta-learning tasks, and  thus the proposed experiment consists in learning a self-contained meta-learner - a meta-meta-learning  experiment, as proposed (but not implemented) by several authors before. 

Importantly, we are *not* proposing a new meta-learning algorithm to learn this or that specific cognitive task (or even a fixed set of such tasks). Rather, we want to produce a self-contained agent capable of automatically *acquiring* such tasks, including novel ones not seen during evolution, from stimuli alone, through the operation of its own machinery. 

Our results demonstrate the feasibility of this process. Importantly, all three levels of learning are important for the success of the experiment (Figure A2, Section 3.3, Appendix C).  

* A common criticism among reviewers is that the tasks being used here do not constitute true meta-learning tasks; that the lowest level (the trial/episode loop)  does not involve actual learning; and thus the scheme is just meta-learning with evolution of plastic networks, which is obviously not novel  (several examples are cited in the submission).

We believe this criticism is incorrect. To the contrary, we emphasize that the tasks used here do constitute  meta-learning tasks,  and are not just analogous, but in some cases exactly identical to well-known meta-learning tasks from the literature. 

Consider the seminal Harlow task (few-shot identification of which of a pair of object is associated with reward), but with only 2 trials per episode, and using the same 2 objects for the whole experiment. Suppose also that the first choice is passive, in that the chosen object is picked at random by the experimenter under the monkey's view, rather than by the monkey itself. The monkey must then pick an object in the second trial, and receives reward (food) if it chose the right object, as in the standard Harlow task. We believe these modifications do not affect the fundamental meta-learning nature of the task: they merely reduce the relevant dimensionality of stimuli and shorten each episode.

Yet this task is not just analogous, but *exactly identical* to our "delayed match-to-sample" task. The first binary stimulus represents which of the two objects is uncovered in the first trial. The second  binary stimulus represents whether or not some food is present under that object. And the agent's response represents which object is selected at the second trial. As  the reviewers can verify, the correct response is exactly identical to that of the DMS task. (Note that in this view, each episode compresses two trials rather than just one.) We have added this comparison in Appendix E.

We believe a source of confusion is the extreme simplification of the stimuli. But the simplified stimuli, which abstract away the need for perceptual processing, do not affect the basic process of meta-learning: unpredictable information must be memorized and adequately processed by the system for each new trial/episode, and how to perform this storing and processing is then learned between episodes in the outer (here, middle) loop. 

Importantly, the (binarized) Yang framework is not just computationally convenient: it also allows us to implement a  wide variety of such simple meta-tasks. Omniglot and 2-trials Harlow are just two tasks. But the Yang framework, even simplified to binary stimuli, immediately produces 16 different meta-tasks. The low computational cost allows us to perform many trials/episodes in reasonable time, despite modest resources. These two aspects (variety of tasks and computational efficiency) are the crucial elements which allow for an outermost "design" loop (here, evolutionary), iterating over many lifetimes.

replying_to: Replying to General reply to reviewers

content.comment:
Dear reviewers,

We have now replied to all reviewers. We would be grateful if reviewers could acknowledge whether they have seen the response, and whether it addressed some of their concerns.

replying_to: Replying to General reply to reviewers

content.title: Thank you for your response!
content.comment:
I really appreciate the authors' detailed response and revisions to the paper. I think the paper has been improved.

Unfortunately, I am still not convinced that the proposed task qualifies as a meta-learning task. The authors argue that the delayed match to sample task is equivalent to a special case of the Harlow task. However, in the Harlow task interpretation of delayed match to sample, the monkey 1) observes an object, 2) discovers if food is under the object and 3) picks the object for the next trial. Importantly, *there is no change in the objects themselves.* In the full Harlow task, the object itself changes across episodes, so the monkey must learn to learn the rewarded object quickly and *generalize across objects.* I don't think delayed match to sample can be considered meta-learning- it's merely learning which object is associated with the reward, not an abstract rule for learning arbitrary object-reward associations.

I don't view the issue with the task as it being too simple; I think trying to simplify the task to its key components as actually valuable. Rather, I think the task omits key elements of the Harlow task that make it a meta-learning task. As an alternative simple example of a meta-learning task, consider the following:

A monkey observes a *single* object during each trial which is associated with reward or not and must decide whether to select the object or not.

Obs 1: Which object the monkey observes for trial 1

Obs 2: Whether the object is associated with reward for trial 1

Obs 3: Which object the monkey observes for trial 2

Action: Whether the monkey picks the observed object

As some example desired associations:

100 -> 1

101 -> 0

001 -> 1

000 -> 0

Observe that in contrast to the delayed match to sample task, the monkey must *generalize* to unobserved objects: if the monkey observes object 0 during trial 1, it may need to infer the reward for (unobserved) object 1 during trial 2. In delayed match-to-sample, the monkey is asked to output the encoding of the object that produced the reward during trial 1 (and the opposite of the encoding if it was unrewarded during trial 1); it is not asked to generalize. 

Of course, in the simply binary setting, all these tasks are just mappings from binary strings to binary values, and thus appear similar. However, one can imagine replacing the binary encoding of observations with images. Then, in delayed match to sample, an image of an object appears along with an indicator of whether or not the object is associated with reward. The monkey must then output an encoding of the object it would like to select. Observe that here, the monkey is not being asked to generalize within an episode; I don't view it as meta-learning.

By contrast, for the proposed task above, the monkey would be given two objects, a reward signal for the first object and be asked whether the second object is associated with the reward signal or not. Here, the monkey must generalize across objects to perform the task since it will in general not have observed the second object during the episode.

I hope the authors will be able to clarify how they consider their proposed task a meta-learning task.

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for your response!

content.title: Response
content.comment:
First, we greatly appreciate the author engaging in such depth with our response.

If we understand correctly, the author's proposed alternative is to augment the DMS task with an additional stimulus-dependent response: after the two first stimuli, instead of immediately outputting a response, the agent is faced with one of the two objects and must decide whether to pick it or not. 

We have two answers for this.

1) The defining characteristic of meta-learning, in our understanding, is that some unpredictable piece of information must be acquired, stored and processed adequately during each episode; while how to do this correctly is learned slowly between episodes. 

To our understanding, in the authors' proposed experiment, the actual information content that must be learned for each episode is *exactly identical* to that of the DMS task / 2-trial Harlow task: it is a binary value that is fully knowable after the second stimulus, and fully determines appropriate behavior for the rest of the episode.

As far as we understand, the main difference lies in *how* this episodic information is to be expressed.  In DMS/2-trial Harlow, this binary learned information must be used to pick directly between two responses: "respond 0"  vs   "respond 1". In the reviewer's proposed alternative, IWUC, the acquired information must be used to select between two stimulus-dependent rules: "if see 0 then pick, if see 1 then don't pick" vs. the reverse.

We agree that this represents an increase in complexity and a more interesting behavior. We are not sure that this difference in processing type should somehow constitute the litmus test for "being meta-learning or not" - considering that the actual data being learned within each episode is exactly the same! The difference in behavior would be entirely an outer-loop matter: the outer loop would need to equip the agent with two stimulus-dependent rules rather than just two different responses. But, in our opinion, this is a difference of degree in complexity rather than a radical break in nature.

2) It appears that the task proposed by the author is immediately usable in our framework, if we simply expand the episode loop to have three stimuli rather than two. By including a third binary stimulus, we would greatly expand the number of possible tasks (from 16 to 256), and  one of them would be exactly the one proposed by the author, IWUC (except that thee third stimulus would also need to be memorized over a delay rather than immediately acted upon).  In fact, this task (and its mirror image) would be a great candidate for withheld task in this additional experiment.

We find it rather counter-intuitive that the fundamental difference between "meta-learning" vs. "not meta-learning" should lie in just having three stimuli rather than two!

Of course, if the reviewer requests it as a condition for acceptance, we would be happy to extend our model to use three stimuli rather than two in each episode and use the reviewers' proposed task as a withheld task  (time constraints permitting). However, we respectfully reiterate that, in our opinion, the author's suggested experiment represents an interesting increase in degree of complexity, but does not seem to alter  the fundamental nature of the overall problem - "learning how to learn something".

It is of course possible  that we misunderstood the reviewer's intent. At any rate, we would be happy to answer any further question or comment by the reviewer.

display_title: Thank you for your detailed response!

content.title: Thank you for your detailed response!
content.comment:
I appreciate the authors' thoughtful comments.

Indeed, I agree with the authors that if meta-learning is defined as "using acquired information to select between stimulus-dependent rules", it is quite counter-intuitive that the three stimulus task could be interpreted as "meta-learning" while the two stimulus task is interpreted as "not meta-learning." However, this can be explained by the observation that even the three stimulus task could also be interpreted as "not meta-learning" since it is merely stimulus-response mapping from 3 bits to 1 bit. Indeed, arguably any meta-learning task can be interpreted as a stimulus-response mapping. In my view, the difference between when a task is considered "meta-learning" vs "not meta-learning" lies in the interpretation of the inputs. If the inputs can be interpreted in such a way that the learner must perform some kind of generalization across different components of the input, then that seems like meta-learning to me. Unfortunately, I'm not convinced there is such an interpretation for the DMS task.

Perhaps the more fundamental issue is that the authors' definition of meta-learning (namely, "some unpredictable piece of information must be acquired, stored and processed adequately during each episode") seems imprecise and overly inclusive. For instance, even MNIST arguably could be considered such a task: pixels in the image must be acquired, stored and processed adequately to produce the correct classification. Yet, MNIST is generally considered a learning task, not a meta-learning task. The boundary at which a task becomes a meta-learning task seems unclear to me. For example, if the stimuli in the DMS task were presented in parallel and not sequentially, would the authors consider it a meta-learning task?

Thus, even if the authors are able to expand the episode loop from 2 to 3 stimuli or more (which would be very valuable), it will also be important to properly frame the task as a meta-learning task and explain the key distinction (if there is one) between learning and meta-learning.

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for your detailed response!

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Once again, we thank the reviewer for taking the time to comment so thoroughly on our response.

> For instance, even MNIST arguably could be considered such a task: pixels in the image must be acquired, stored and processed adequately to produce the correct classification. Yet, MNIST is generally considered a learning task, not a meta-learning task. The boundary at which a task becomes a meta-learning task seems unclear to me. For example, if the stimuli in the DMS task were presented in parallel and not sequentially, would the authors consider it a meta-learning task?

We note that neither of these two tasks involve any memory in the agent, much less mental manipulation of memorized information. They're pure stimulus-response behaviors, and thus cannot possibly involve "learning-to-learn" - there is no second "learn" here by *any* definition. 

We believe our definition to be reasonably usable: it is generally quite unambiguous whether a task requires working memory and mental processing or not. 

However, it seems that the difference in opinion runs deeper, as we note next.

> If the inputs can be interpreted in such a way that the learner must perform some kind of generalization across different components of the input, then that seems like meta-learning to me.

Perhaps the reviewer means "generalizing over  different kinds of stimuli/objects from one episode to the next", rather than within episodes (as we evidently misunderstood)? But for us, while learning generalizing representations is an important problem, it is a perceptual problem, quite separate from the cognitive one  (storing, manipulating and exploiting novel information) which we feel is the relevant aspect.

It is quite possible that we unwittingly stumbled upon a true difference of opinion about what counts as meta-learning here:

Consider the Harlow task, but using always the same two objects over all episodes (what changes from one episode to the next is which of the two objects contains the food). Does this task constitute "meta-learning"? For the reviewer, presumably, it wouldn't: since the same two objects are being used, there is no generalization over new object sets - it is in a sense "always the same thing". But for us, it absolutely is meta-learning, because some information is learned and processed within each episode, and how to do this is learned slowly between episodes; generalizing over different pairs of objects is a perceptual addition to the main cognitive process being meta-learned, which is the important one for us.

We are of course willing to acknowledge the difference of opinion and qualify the term meta-meta-learning in the paper. We're unsure whether this difference be grounds for withholding publication in the face of the paper's actual results (evolving a self-contained agent capable of automatically acquiring novel, simple cognitive tasks).

We remain ready to answer any further comments or question by the reviewer.

display_title: Thank you for your detailed response!

content.title: Thank you for your detailed response!
content.comment:
I appreciate your insightful response.

As I understand it, the authors propose as a criteria for meta-learning any task that requires: 1) storage of information across multiple time steps and 2) manipulation of the stored information to produce a response. 

Indeed, it appears that we have a fundamental difference of opinion on what counts as meta-learning. In my view, the Harlow task with two objects does not count as meta-learning in the sense that all episodes are identical (up to the random selection of which object has the reward). The equivalent in Omniglot would be if all the alphabets in Omniglot were the same.

One question I have for the authors is whether they would consider the following task meta-learning: consider a version of MNIST where each pixel is fed sequentially over time to an agent which must produce a predicted digit after viewing all pixels. As I understand it, such a version of MNIST would be considered a meta-learning task according to the authors.

In any case, I think the relevant point to discuss is not the definition of meta-learning (I'm happy to agree that the paper indeed performs meta-meta-learning under the authors' definition); it is whether method proposed by the authors can extend to more complex cognitive meta-learning tasks. As I understand it, the authors consider DMS-style tasks under the belief that they share a common underlying structure with other, more complex meta-learning tasks, and thus being able to acquire DMS-style tasks is an important step to being able to acquire general cognitive meta-learning tasks.

Thus, one key question is whether the approach outlined in this paper can be practically extended to a task like Omniglot (which we both can agree is a meta-learning task). If the difference between Omniglot and the DMS-style tasks is merely perceptual complexity, then I would expect that the proposed approach could be used to solve at least a simplified version of Omniglot. If there is a more fundamental difference, then I would expect that the proposed approach may not work. I think some kind of empirical validation of this would be really valuable.

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for your detailed response!

content.title: Response
content.comment:
> In any case, I think the relevant point to discuss is not the definition of meta-learning

We agree with that. The upshot is that it is not  easy to find a definition of meta-learning that includes Omniglot, bandits, etc. while excluding sequential  MNIST (variable stimuli across episodes cannot suffice, since it also applies to sequential MNIST).

>  it is whether method proposed by the authors can extend to more complex cognitive meta-learning tasks. 

We fully agree that implementing more complex tasks is a priority for future work. One difficulty is that it isn't  enough to just implement a low-dimensional Omniglot, or Harlow, or bandits, etc. Rather, we need a whole variety of meta tasks, using a  common framework, which would somehow include Omniglot / bandits/ etc within their  configuration space.. The Yang set of simple cognitive tasks offered such a variety at low computational costs, and is becoming a kind of standard in computational neuroscience, which is why it seemed like an obvious first step.

We thank the reviewer for this in-depth discussion of the relevant issues.
